contradictions.question: Is a good name a blessing or curse?
contradictions.summary: The wisdom tradition treats a good reputation as one of life's highest goods. Ecclesiastes 7:1 ranks a good name above precious ointment and Proverbs 22:1 ranks it above great riches. Luke 6:26 flips the valuation — Jesus pronounces a woe on those of whom all speak well, on the grounds that the same kind of universal approval was given to the false prophets. The shared term is reputation, but the Hebrew sages prize it and the Lukan Jesus treats it as a danger sign.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real at the level of how each text evaluates public esteem, but it lives in the gap between two distinct genres and theological programs. Ecclesiastes 7:1 and Proverbs 22:1 belong to the mainstream Israelite wisdom tradition, where shem tov — a good name — is the social capital that signals a life lived in alignment with the moral order. Qoheleth even pushes the idea farther: a good name plus the day of death is preferable to perfume plus the day of birth, because reputation is the only thing that outlasts you. Proverbs 22:1 grounds the same valuation in shame-honor logic — favor and reputation outrank wealth. Luke 6:26 stands in a completely different stream. It is the fourth and final woe in the Lukan Sermon on the Plain, an inversion-of-fortunes counterpart to the beatitude in Luke 6:22-23, where the disciples are blessed when men hate them and cast out their name as evil for the Son of Man's sake. The Lukan logic is prophetic-eschatological: in a corrupt world, universal approval is evidence that you are saying what people want to hear, exactly like the court prophets of Ahab and the false prophets denounced by Jeremiah and Micah. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by distinguishing between a good name earned by righteous conduct and a good name earned by sycophancy, and the distinction is genuine — but the harmonization papers over the fact that the wisdom texts make no such qualification. They treat the universal good report as straightforwardly desirable. Luke's Jesus treats it as straightforwardly dangerous. The tension is not nominal; it reflects a real shift from sapiential ethics to apocalyptic-prophetic ethics within the canon.

contradictions.question: Is there a remedy for foolishness?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 22:15 and Proverbs 27:22 sit in the same book and give opposite verdicts on whether foolishness can be driven out of a person. 22:15 says foolishness is bound in the heart of a child but the rod of correction will drive it far from him — corporal discipline as the cure. 27:22 says you can grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with wheat and his foolishness still will not depart from him — the fool is incorrigible. Same wisdom collection, two incompatible anthropologies of folly.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in Proverbs and it shows up because Proverbs is not a unified treatise but an anthology of distinct collections — at minimum the Solomonic core in chapters 10-22:16, the Sayings of the Wise in 22:17-24:34, the Hezekian collection in 25-29, and the appendices of Agur and Lemuel in 30-31. Different collections, different sages, different views of human nature. The Solomonic collection (which contains 22:15) is optimistic about the formative power of discipline: the rod of musar drives folly out of the child because folly is acquired, not constitutive. The Hezekian collection (which contains 27:22) is closer to the worldview of Qoheleth — folly is an essence, a kind of fixed disposition that no amount of external pressure can dislodge. The image of grinding a fool in a mortar with a pestle is deliberately absurd, the kind of hyperbole that makes the point that even total bodily violence cannot expel the trait. Apologists like Bruce Waltke harmonize by appealing to age — 22:15 applies to children whose character is still being formed, while 27:22 applies to mature fools whose character is set. That is a defensible reading and it does relieve the surface tension, but it requires you to import age categories that the text itself does not specify. Both verses speak generically of the fool (kesil / 'evil) without restricting the proverb to a developmental stage. The more parsimonious reading is that the redactors of Proverbs preserved competing voices from the wisdom schools — one that believed in the malleability of character through discipline, one that did not — and made no attempt to harmonize them. That is exactly what we should expect from an anthology, and exactly what the form-critical work of Whybray and Fox has been arguing for decades.

contradictions.question: Is temptation desired?
contradictions.summary: James 1:2 tells believers to count it all joy when they fall into various peirasmoi — testings or temptations — because the testing of faith produces endurance. Matthew 6:13, the petition embedded in the Lord's Prayer, asks the Father not to lead us into peirasmos but to deliver us from evil. The lexical overlap is exact: the same Greek word peirasmos is the object of celebration in James and the object of avoidance in the Lord's Prayer. One source says embrace it, the other says ask God to spare you from it.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction hinges on the Greek word peirasmos, which spans the semantic range from outward trial to inward solicitation to sin. James 1:2 opens his epistle by reframing peirasmoi as occasions for joy because the dokimion (testing) of pistis works endurance — the trial is instrumental in maturing the believer. Matthew 6:13, embedded in the Lord's Prayer, takes the opposite stance — me eisenenkes hemas eis peirasmon, do not bring us into peirasmos. The petition treats peirasmos as something to be avoided, not embraced. Apologists like Douglas Moo and D. A. Carson typically harmonize by claiming the two passages use peirasmos in different senses — James means external trial (testing of faith) while Matthew means inner enticement to sin. The distinction is grammatically defensible but exegetically thin. James 1:13 in fact switches to the inner sense within the same paragraph, saying God tempts no one to evil, which means James knows the dual sense and uses both. Matthew 6:13 includes no qualifier that would restrict its peirasmos to enticement-only. The petition is general and asks for deliverance from the situation itself, not for strength to resist enticement within it. Pope Francis's 2019 retranslation of the Italian missal (to render it as do not let us fall into temptation rather than lead us not into temptation) is essentially an acknowledgment that the plain reading creates exactly this difficulty — it makes God the agent of leading believers into peirasmos, which is theologically intolerable. The honest reading is that James and Matthew represent different early Christian postures toward suffering and trial: James embraces it as paideia, Matthew prays for exemption from it. Same word, opposite responses.

contradictions.question: Is prophecy a sure thing?
contradictions.summary: 2 Peter 1:19 calls the prophetic word more sure (bebaioteron) — a lamp shining in a dark place that the faithful do well to heed. Jeremiah 18:7-10 makes prophecy explicitly conditional: if Yahweh declares destruction against a nation and that nation repents, he will relent; if he declares blessing and that nation does evil, he will withdraw the blessing. 2 Peter treats prophecy as fixed and reliable; Jeremiah treats it as contingent on human response. The two passages disagree on whether prophetic announcements are predictions of fixed outcomes or conditional warnings.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real but it operates at a slightly different level than the proof-texts suggest. 2 Peter 1:19 is using prophecy in a Christological sense — the prophetic word that points to the parousia, validated for the author by the transfiguration tradition cited in the preceding verses. The author's claim is that this Christological prophetic witness is bebaioteron, more firm or reliable, than even the voice from heaven. Jeremiah 18:7-10, embedded in the potter-and-clay oracle, is making a fundamentally different claim about how prophetic announcements work in the political and moral economy of Israel and the nations. They are not fixed predictions; they are responsive declarations. Yahweh announces, the nation responds, Yahweh adjusts. This is the same theological logic that allows Jonah to complain in 4:2 that he knew all along Yahweh would relent over Nineveh — because that is how prophecy works in the Deuteronomistic and Jeremianic theological streams. Apologists like Walter Kaiser harmonize by distinguishing between unconditional prophecies (the messianic promises, the new covenant) and conditional prophecies (oracles of judgment against nations), and the distinction does have textual support — Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 both insist Yahweh is not a man that he should repent, while Jeremiah 18 and Jonah 3-4 insist that he does. The honest reading is that the Hebrew Bible itself contains two competing views on whether prophetic announcement is fixed or conditional, and Jeremiah 18:7-10 represents the conditional view while later prophetic and apocalyptic texts move toward the fixed view. 2 Peter, working within the fixed view, says prophecy is sure. Jeremiah, working within the conditional view, says prophecy is contingent. Apologists are right that the contradiction is not quite a flat yes/no, but they are wrong to deny that the two streams represent genuinely different prophetic anthropologies. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the textual data points hard in that direction.

contradictions.question: Is every animal afraid of man?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 9:2, embedded in the post-flood Noachic covenant, has Yahweh place the fear and dread (morakem ve-hittekem) of human beings upon every beast of the earth, every bird of the sky, every creeping thing, and every fish of the sea — they are delivered into human hands. Proverbs 30:30 says the lion is strongest among beasts and turns away from no one. The Genesis text is a universal claim about every beast; Proverbs offers a counter-example that explicitly exempts at least one species.
contradictions.commentary: This is the kind of contradiction that exists mainly at the level of rhetorical scope rather than narrative substance, and it pays to be honest about that. Genesis 9:2 belongs to the Priestly post-flood narrative and functions theologically — humans are re-authorized after the flood as the dominant ecological force, with carnivory now permitted (9:3) and animal fear of humanity instituted as the means of that dominance. The verse is making a programmatic statement about the post-flood order, not a zoological prediction that no animal will ever attack a human. Proverbs 30:30 sits inside Agur's numerical sayings (30:24-31) and is making a different kind of claim entirely — it is observational wisdom literature cataloging examples of stately or fearless creatures (the lion, the strutting rooster, the male goat, the king with his army), with the lion as exhibit A of an animal that does not retreat. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by noting that morakem in Genesis 9:2 expresses a general principle of the post-flood order rather than an absolute exemption from any animal aggression, and that Proverbs 30:30 is poetic observation, not a denial of the Genesis principle. That is fair as far as it goes — the Genesis text is using totalizing language for theological emphasis. But it is also true that the totalizing language of Genesis 9:2 (every beast, every bird, every creeping thing) sets up an expectation that Proverbs 30:30 specifically refuses. Apologetically, the harmonization works. Textually, the two passages stand in tension. The more parsimonious reading is that Genesis 9:2 is a theological-mythic claim about cosmic order while Proverbs 30:30 is empirical observation, and the Israelite canon preserves both without trying to reconcile them. Whether that constitutes a contradiction depends on how literally you want to take the language of Genesis 9:2 — and the inerrantist position requires you to take it very literally indeed.

contradictions.question: Are miracles proof of divine mission?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 11:2-5 has Jesus point to his miracles — blind seeing, lame walking, lepers cleansed, deaf hearing, dead raised — as the answer to John the Baptist's question whether he is the coming one. John 3:2 has Nicodemus reason backward from Jesus' signs to the conclusion that no one could do them unless God were with him. Exodus 14:31 grounds Israelite faith in Moses in the great work at the Red Sea. The opposing side cites Exodus 7:10-12, where Pharaoh's magicians replicate Aaron's serpent-rod sign with their enchantments, Deuteronomy 13:1-3, which explicitly commands Israel to reject a prophet whose sign or wonder comes to pass if he calls them to other gods, and Luke 11:19, where Jesus concedes that Jewish exorcists also cast out demons. Miracles are evidentiary in the first set; the second set says miracles do not settle the question of divine authorization.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction operates at the level of evidentiary epistemology and it is one of the more interesting ones in the canon because both sides are right about something. The pro-miracle stream — Matthew 11, John 3, Exodus 14 — treats sign-events as warrants for prophetic or messianic identity. The Matthean Jesus deflects John's question by reciting a list of healings that echoes Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1, framing the miracles as the fulfillment of messianic prophecy. The Johannine semeia theology is even more explicit — the signs are the basis on which the reader is asked to believe (John 20:30-31). Exodus 14:31 turns the Red Sea event into the foundation of Israel's covenant faith in Yahweh and Moses. But the counter-stream is just as clear. Exodus 7:10-12 puts the Egyptian magicians on the same evidentiary footing as Aaron — they too can produce serpents — which means the sign-event alone does not establish whose god is real. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 makes this explicit at the level of legal principle: even a fulfilled sign or wonder does not authenticate a prophet if his message contradicts covenant fidelity. Luke 11:19 has Jesus himself concede that Jewish exorcists who are not his disciples also perform exorcisms, which means exorcistic power is not by itself proof of his unique authorization. Apologists like Norman Geisler and Craig Blomberg harmonize by distinguishing between genuine and counterfeit miracles, arguing that Pharaoh's magicians performed lesser or demonic signs while Aaron's was true divine power, and that Deuteronomy 13 only applies when the prophet's message is heretical. The distinction is theologically convenient but exegetically strained — the Exodus narrative does not say the magicians' serpents were illusions or demonic; it says they did so as Aaron did, in like manner. The more parsimonious reading is that the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament both contain a more sophisticated epistemology than the pro-miracle proof-texts suggest. Miracles function as evidence in some contexts and are explicitly disqualified as standalone evidence in others. The contradiction is real at the level of any flat claim that miracles prove divine mission — Deuteronomy 13:1-3 is the smoking gun against that thesis, and it is in the same Torah that grounds Mosaic authority in the Red Sea sign.
